## 3.1.1 Research problem and empirical design

Both abstracts have a clear problem → experiment → result structure, although KYC is more direct.

KYC firstly states the practical problem that applying VLMs end-to-end to long scanned financial documents is unreliable and error prone. So it links an industrial extraction problem to a pipeline, baseline comparisons and component ablations.

On the other hand, VAREX states the problem is in existing benchmarks, that normally evaluate one input representation, making it difficult to determine whether performance depends on the model or on how the document is represented.

VAREX therefore gives more information about the structure of its experiment, while KYC gives a simpler connection between the practical problem, proposed solution and measured outcome.

## 3.1.2 Validity and credibility of the claims

For internal validity, VAREX use different document representations to inference if it causes a difference in extraction performance, since document content is kept constant. In KYC, removing a single component can support the claim that component contributes to the performance, but we cannot conclude that it is the only explanation; we do not know how other components could interact with the excluded one.

Regarding construct validity, VAREX claims small models fail due output compliance rather than extraction capabilities. But the applied solution, fine-tuning, can potentially improve both aspects. From the abstract alone it is harder to prove exactly which underlying capability improved. KYC has a smaller gap between observation and interpretation: removing retrieval reduces performance, so retrieval likely contributes to the result. However field-level accuracy could not represent the total extraction quality.

For statistical validity, we do not have enough elements from the abstracts. KYC is easier to interpret because it gives an absolute score. However, neither abstract reports confidence intervals or another measure of uncertainty, especially important with nondeterministic nature of LLMs.

## 3.1.3 Realism, generalisability and precision

KYC connects the substantive problem directly with the method: it studies industrial KYC extraction using production documents. VAREX connects the conceptual question with the method: it wants to study input representation conditioning and therefore creates controlled versions of the same documents.

Following McGrath, the different strengths of KYC and VAREX can also be understood as methodological trade-offs: KYC provides more realism using real-world documents, while VAREX provides more control and precision creating a synthetic dataset to test different input format.

## 3.2 Conclusion

Overall, I find the KYC abstract slightly clearer and more credible in how it communicates its empirical research. Its problem, intervention, experiment and conclusion form a very direct chain.

VAREX is strong in describing its experimental control and benchmark construction, and its matched representations make the input-modality comparison particularly convincing. However, because the study reports a broad experiment and four distinct findings, the abstract has limited space to explain each result in detail.

## References and source abstracts

- [1] Han, Y., Zhang, Y., Wang, Y., & Jin, Y. (2026). A Multistage Extraction Pipeline for Long Scanned Financial Documents: An Empirical Study in Industrial KYC Workflows. In Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 6: Industry Track (pp. 1419-1433). Association for Computational Linguistics. DOI: 10.18653/v1/2026.acl-industry.99.

ACL Anthology (CC BY 4.0)

Structured information extraction from long, multilingual scanned financial documents is a core requirement in industrial KYC and compliance workflows. These documents are typically non-machinereadable, noisy, and visually heterogeneous. They usually span dozens of pages while containing only sparse task-relevant information. Although recent vision-language models (VLMs) achieve strong benchmark performance, directly applying them end-to-end to full financial reports often leads to unreliable extraction under real-world conditions.

We evaluated the framework on 120 production KYC documents comprising about 3000 multilingual scanned pages. Across multiple OCR-VLM combinations, the proposed pipeline consistently outperforms direct PDF-to-VLM baselines, improving field-level accuracy by up to 31.9 percentage points. The best configuration, PaddleOCR with MiniCPM-o-2.6, achieves 87.27% accuracy. Ablation studies show that page-level retrieval is the dominant factor in performance improvements, particularly for complex financial statements and non-English documents.

We present a multistage extraction framework that integrates image preprocessing, multilingual OCR, hybrid page-level retrieval, and compact VLM-based structured extraction. The design separates page localization from multimodal reasoning, enabling more accurate extraction from complex multi-page documents.

- [2] Barzelay, U., Azulai, O., Shapira, I., Friedman, I., Abo Dahood, F., Lee, M., & Daniels, A. (2026). VAREX: A Benchmark for Multi-Modal Structured Extraction from Documents. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) Workshops (pp. 7368-7376).

[CVF Open Access: published CVPR Workshops version](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026W/MMFM5/html/Barzelay_VAREX_A_Benchmark_for_Multi-Modal_Structured_Extraction_from_Documents_CVPRW_2026_paper.html)

We introduce VAREX (VARied-schema EXtraction), a benchmark for evaluating multimodal foundation models on structured data extraction from government forms. VAREX employs a Reverse Annotation pipeline that programmatically fills PDF templates with synthetic values, producing deterministic ground truth validated through three-phase quality assurance. The benchmark comprises 1,798 documents with unique per-document schemas across three structural categories, each provided in four input modalities: plain text, layout-preserving text (whitespace-aligned to approximate column positions), document image, or both text and image combined. Unlike existing benchmarks that evaluate from a single input representation, VAREX provides four controlled modalities per document, enabling systematic ablation of how input format affects extraction accuracy - a capability absent from prior benchmarks. We evaluate 20 models from frontier proprietary models to small open models, with particular attention to models ≤ 4B parameters suitable for cost-sensitive and latency-constrained deployment. Results reveal that (1) below 4B parameters, structured output compliance - not extraction capability - is a dominant bottleneck; in particular, schema echo (models reproducing the schema definition instead of extracting values) depresses scores by 45-65 pp (percentage points) in affected models; (2) extraction-specific fine-tuning at 2B yields +81 pp gains, demonstrating that the instruction-following deficit is addressable without scale; (3) layout-preserving text provides the largest accuracy gain (+3-18 pp), exceeding pixel-level visual cues; and (4) the benchmark most effectively discriminates models in the 60-95% accuracy band.
